planting.note: Set out rooted divisions or cuttings after the last frost into consistently moist, fertile soil; propagate only vegetatively, as peppermint is a sterile hybrid that does not come true from seed.

directions: White peppermint is the paler-stemmed botanical form of Mentha x piperita, lacking the purple-red pigmentation of black peppermint and carrying a lighter green leaf and a milder, less pungent menthol flavor. It is favored where a softer peppermint note is wanted, such as in delicate teas and light confections, and was historically grown alongside black peppermint in commercial oil fields as a distinct strain. Contain its spreading rhizomes with a buried barrier or a sunken pot, and keep the soil evenly moist through the growing season for the best leaf quality. Cut plants back hard after flowering to renew tender growth for a second harvest before frost.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; part of the University of Minnesota's Mammoth series bred for reliable perennial survival without winter mulch as far north as zone 3.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Mammoth Red Daisy forms a naturally rounded, dense mound and does not require pinching to stay compact. It bears single, daisy-form deep red flowers with yellow centers in a heavy late-summer to early-fall flush, timed early enough to bloom reliably even in short-season northern gardens. Bred at the University of Minnesota for exceptional cold hardiness, it survives winters in the open ground without mulching where many florist-type mums fail. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; like other Mammoth-series mums it is bred at the University of Minnesota for perennial survival without winter mulch as far north as zone 3.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Mammoth Coral Daisy grows into a dense, self-branching mound without pinching. Warm coral-salmon single daisy flowers with yellow centers cover the plant in a heavy late-summer to early-fall display, blooming early enough to color up before hard frost in cold climates. Its University of Minnesota breeding gives it outstanding winter hardiness compared to typical greenhouse-grown florist mums. Lift and divide overgrown clumps every two to three years in spring.

scientific_name: Chrysanthemum x morifolium 'Mammoth Dark Purple Daisy'

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; developed by the University of Minnesota breeding program for survival without winter mulch as far north as zone 3.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Mammoth Dark Purple Daisy forms a tidy, naturally mounded plant that needs no pinching to stay full and compact. Rich violet-purple single daisy flowers with contrasting yellow centers appear in a dense late-summer to early-fall flush, blooming reliably even where seasons are short. Its University of Minnesota parentage gives the roots exceptional cold tolerance, allowing the plant to overwinter in the ground unprotected in far colder climates than typical garden mums. Divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring to renew vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; bred at the University of Minnesota for perennial survival without winter mulch as far north as zone 3.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Mammoth Lavender Daisy builds a dense, rounded mound on its own without pinching. Soft lavender-purple single daisy flowers with bright yellow centers open in a heavy late-summer to early-fall flush, timed to bloom well ahead of hard freezes in cold-winter gardens. As part of the University of Minnesota's cold-hardy mum breeding program, it returns reliably year after year without winter protection where many pot mums die out. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; part of the University of Minnesota's Mammoth series bred for reliable survival without winter mulch as far north as zone 3.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Mammoth Yellow Quill grows into a full, self-branching mound without any pinching required. Its distinctive golden-yellow flowers have narrow, quilled petals rather than the flat daisy form of other Mammoth-series mums, giving plants a spiky, textured look in the late-summer to early-fall bloom flush. Bred at the University of Minnesota, it carries the same outstanding cold-hardy rootstock as the rest of the series, overwintering successfully without mulch in far colder regions than typical garden center mums. Lift and divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Mammoth White Daisy forms a dense, naturally rounded mound that stays full without pinching. Crisp white single daisy flowers with bright yellow centers open in a heavy late-summer to early-fall flush, blooming early enough to put on a full show before hard frost even in short-season climates. Its University of Minnesota parentage gives it the same exceptional root hardiness as the rest of the Mammoth series, allowing it to overwinter unprotected well north of where florist-type mums survive. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep plants vigorous.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors 6-8 weeks early for earlier bloom; press seed onto the soil surface since it needs light to germinate.

directions: Autumn Colors is an open-pollinated seed strain that trades the solid gold of the wild black-eyed Susan for a warm mix of bronze, mahogany, rust, and gold tones, often banded or bicolor, on single daisy-form flowers around a dark chocolate-brown cone. Grow in full sun and average, well-drained soil; plants tolerate heat and short dry spells better than most bedding annuals once established. Deadhead regularly through summer to keep new buds coming, or leave some seed heads to mature for reliable self-sowing and a repeat color mix the following year. The tall, branching stems make good cut flowers and the varied autumnal palette suits informal cottage and prairie-style plantings.

common_name: Toto Gold Black-Eyed Susan (AAS-Winning Dark-Eyeless Dwarf Rudbeckia)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost for earliest bloom, or direct sow once soil has warmed; Toto Gold was an All-America Selections winner prized for its extra-dwarf, uniform habit.

directions: Toto Gold breaks from the classic black-eyed Susan look by producing solid, glowing golden-yellow flowers with little to no dark central disc, set on an especially compact and uniform plant even shorter than the original Toto. Its tidy, mounded habit and early, heavy bloom made it an All-America Selections winner, and it excels in containers, edging, and mass bedding where consistent height matters. Grow in full sun and moderately fertile, well-drained soil, watering regularly during establishment for the most continuous bloom. Deadheading is optional since the plants stay floriferous through summer heat with minimal grooming.

common_name: Toto Rustic Black-Eyed Susan (AAS-Winning Mahogany-Toned Dwarf Rudbeckia)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow after frost danger passes; Toto Rustic shares the extra-dwarf, uniform Toto habit but in warmer mahogany-bronze tones.

directions: Toto Rustic pairs the same extra-compact, uniform mounding habit that made the Toto series an award winner with warm mahogany, bronze, and burnt-orange ray petals surrounding a dark central cone, a departure from the solid golds of most dwarf black-eyed Susans. Its small, tidy size suits containers, edging, and the front of sunny borders where the richer autumnal coloring stands out against green-eyed or plain-gold companions. Grow in full sun and moderately fertile, well-drained soil, and water regularly while plants establish for the heaviest bloom. Flowers hold up well in heat and continue through summer with little deadheading required.
